title: After 40 Years of Silence, Ritchie Blackmore Reunites with Deep Purple for One Emotional Song
summary:
For decades, a Deep Purple reunion with founding guitarist Ritchie Blackmore seemed about as likely as a snowball surviving a summer day. Blackmore left the band acrimoniously in 1993, and as recently as 2014, frontman Ian Gillan told Rolling Stone that bringing him back would be 'unconscionable.' Even at their Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction in 2016, the band refused to let Blackmore play a single song. So when Blackmore announced on Instagram on August 11 that he'd be joining them the next night at Jones Beach, fans were stunned.

In a new interview with Guitar Player, Blackmore revealed the reunion began with a simple morning thought: 'It would be good for the fans if I just got up for one song, probably "Smoke," and just show that we're not at each other's throats.' His wife, Candice, reached out to Gillan, whose exact words were, 'It made me smile.' The rest of the band gave a thumbs-up, and suddenly, a 40-year wall came down.

But the moment was more than just a publicity stunt. Blackmore, 81, suffered a heart attack last year that left him unable to play guitar for months. He had to dust off a Stratocaster he hadn't touched since the 1980s, change the strings, and re-learn a technique he'd abandoned—using a pick instead of his long fingernails. 'I still lost my place at one point,' he admitted, 'but it's not why I was there. I was there to heal any wounds—but there weren't any wounds. Everyone was like, we were in the army, all along the Western front and we were all getting together again. Very emotional moment.'

Gillan echoed that sentiment after the show, posting, 'What a pleasure it was to welcome Ritchie Blackmore on stage with us to play Smoke last night. Thanks Ritchie, that meant a lot to many people; not least me.' While a full reunion tour is unlikely, for one night, the band that once defined hard rock proved that time—and a shared love of music—can mend even the deepest rifts.
why_it_matters: The story matters because it shows how even famous bands carry decades of personal history, and that reconciliation often happens through small symbolic gestures rather than full-scale reunions. For fans, a single song can reshape how a group's legacy is remembered.

background_read: Deep Purple is a pioneering British hard-rock band formed in 1968; its song 'Smoke on the Water' has one of rock's most recognizable guitar riffs.
Ritchie Blackmore was the band's founding guitarist and co-writer of that riff, but he left in 1993 amid angry disputes, and for decades lead singer Ian Gillan said a reunion was unthinkable.
The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, a U.S. institution that honors influential musicians, inducted Deep Purple in 2016, but the group still refused to let Blackmore perform at the ceremony.
Jones Beach is an outdoor amphitheater on New York's Long Island coast, a regular stop for touring rock bands; Blackmore announced on Instagram that he would join the band there for one song.

After a heart attack last year left him unable to play for months, Blackmore restrung an old Stratocaster and used a pick—a technique he had abandoned decades earlier—which made the one-song reunion feel more personal than promotional.

perspectives.perspective: Fans and band members seeking closure
perspectives.description: For many fans, seeing Blackmore play 'Smoke' with Deep Purple again was a healing moment decades in the making. Ian Gillan's public thanks and Blackmore's emotional account suggest the band members themselves wanted to rewrite a bitter ending into a shared memory.

perspectives.perspective: Skeptics who see a publicity stunt or too little, too late
perspectives.description: Some may view the one-song appearance as a publicity move that cannot undo years of exclusion, including the Hall of Fame snub in 2016. Blackmore admitted he lost his place in the song, and a single guest appearance may feel unsatisfying to those who wanted a genuine reunion rather than a symbolic gesture.

perspectives.perspective: The long life of band conflicts
perspectives.description: The story illustrates how personal and artistic conflicts in famous groups can harden over decades, becoming part of their public identity. Even after the band's induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the refusal to let Blackmore play showed that institutional honors do not automatically resolve personal rifts.

perspectives.perspective: What this means for the future of Deep Purple
perspectives.description: The article notes that a full reunion tour is unlikely, so the one-night appearance may be the endpoint rather than the start of a new era. Still, it offers a model for aging rock bands: short, manageable collaborations that acknowledge shared history without reopening old business arrangements.
